title: Tele-Clearance for Sheriffs' Booking Desks
one_liner: A night-shift nurse-and-NP screening service that lets a rural deputy clear an arrestee for booking from the jail, without spending four hours in the ER while the county goes unpatrolled.
customer: County sheriffs and county commissioners, funded through county risk pools and insurers (for example state association-of-counties liability pools) that pay for jail deaths and lawsuits. Paid per county per month.
problem: Rural jails often have no on-site medical staff, so jail policy requires a hospital 'medical clearance' for any arrestee who is intoxicated, injured or says his chest hurts. At 2am the deputy brings the person to the ER and sits with him for 3-5 hours, sometimes the county's only deputy on duty. The county pays a $2,000-4,000 ER bill and has nobody patrolling. The ER meanwhile holds a bed and a nurse for someone with nothing acutely wrong except being drunk. When clearance is skipped, the risk is a death in custody from alcohol or opioid withdrawal, a head injury or diabetic crisis, which is a lawsuit.
solution: A booking-desk kit (vitals, pulse oximeter, glucometer, breathalyzer, tablet) plus 24/7 on-demand video screening by an RN and NP working from home, using a physician-signed clearance protocol built from ACEP's published best-practice guidance for patients in custody. Dispositions are 'fit for booking with monitoring plan', 'needs ER now', or 're-check in 2 hours'. The service also creates a documented withdrawal-watch checklist, such as sobriety and CIWA-style monitoring, which jails need for liability reasons. The report is time-stamped and defensible.
why_now: Rural hospital and ER closures are lengthening transport times. Prison Policy Initiative reported in October 2025 that about half of incarcerated people are held in rural jails and prisons that risk losing hospital access. Medicaid cuts and the pressure on county budgets are also forcing sheriffs to look for cheaper options, and some already release people on 'medical bond' to avoid ER bills. Telehealth billing and licensure flexibility, together with the Nurse Licensure Compact, make cross-state night staffing workable.
revenue_model: $2,000-3,500 per county per month, including up to about 40 screens. Additional screens are $85 each. Roughly 12 counties would support a team of 6 part-time clinicians. Later, sell an outcome dashboard called 'deputy hours returned to patrol', which is the number commissioners and risk-pool underwriters will care about most.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames the problem as ER wait time or inmate healthcare. From inside the ER, the real cost is the deputy who is stuck with us. In a county with one or two deputies on at night, an ER trip is a public safety hole, and the buyer will pay to close it. Also, most 'medical clearances' are defensive medicine that a good screen would make unnecessary. Big correctional health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare) sell staffing for large jails and are not built for a 12-bed jail on a county road.
first_30_days: Write the clearance protocol with a supervising physician from a rural ER and get it reviewed by one county attorney. Choose one sheriff the founder already knows from ER encounters. Run a paid pilot at $1,500 for 60 days and count deputy hours saved and ER trips avoided. Then pitch the state's county risk pool and sheriffs' association with the numbers.

title: Prize-Money Payout and Tax Withholding for Sports Tours
one_liner: A payout engine for pro-am tours and event organizers that KYCs athletes, collects tax forms, withholds correctly on nonresident winners, files the paperwork, and pays in local currency or stablecoin within 24 hours instead of on a 60-day wire.
customer: Organizers of tours and one-off events with international fields and $50k-$5M purses: pickleball, padel, fitness racing such as Hyrox, BJJ and grappling, trail ultras, surf and CrossFit-style competitions. Agents and athlete associations are secondary users.
problem: US-source prize money paid to nonresident athletes is generally subject to 30% withholding unless treaty status is properly documented, with W-8 forms and 1042-S filings. Small organizers mishandle this and carry penalty risk. Athletes wait weeks for wires that cost $25-45 plus FX spread. Athletes in countries like Kenya or Ethiopia often lose another 10-20% to agents, and payments to unbanked winners are a mess.
solution: A payee vault that holds W-8 and W-9 forms, treaty article claims and sanctions screening. The organizer funds the purse by ACH. The engine applies split rules for sponsor, agent, team and coach, calculates withholding by treaty and state, files 1042-S and 1099 forms, and pays out to bank accounts, mobile money or USDC wallets through partners in supported corridors. Payouts can be triggered at the podium. Each payout also creates a verified earnings record for the athlete.
why_now: Independent tours and pro-am leagues have multiplied and raised purses through 2024-26. Stablecoins are now regulated plumbing after the GENIUS Act, with the Fed proposing issuer rules on Sept 24, 2026. Circle's $400M Tazapay deal and Yellow Card's $40M raise are building local payout rails in emerging markets. The 1% US remittance tax on cash-funded transfers pushes senders toward digital rails.
revenue_model: 1.0-1.5% of purse volume, $15-25 per payee onboarding, $10 per 1042-S filed, and an FX spread. A tour paying out $10M a year yields about $150k in revenue.
non_obvious_insight: Sports' payout problem is not moving money, it is proving who is owed what and what to withhold. The rail is a commodity while the compliance file is the moat. Every payout also produces an athlete-verified earnings record, which lets a semi-pro athlete prove income for a bank, visa or insurer, something thin-margin athletes cannot do today.
first_30_days: Pick two fragmented sports with foreign fields, such as a trail-ultra series and a mid-tier pickleball or padel tour. Offer to run payouts for one event at cost. Use a fractional international-tax CPA plus Stripe Connect, Wise or Airwallex for the plumbing. Pre-build a treaty table for the top 30 athlete home countries. Charge 1.5% from the second event onward and aim for five events in 90 days.

title: AV-TEST for Deepfake and Liveness Detectors
one_liner: A buyer-funded independent lab that red-teams deepfake and liveness detectors every month against fresh in-the-wild fakes and publishes procurement-grade scorecards.
customer: Bank and insurer model-risk and fraud-procurement teams, enterprise CISOs buying detection, media organizations, and expert witnesses. All buy annual subscriptions.
problem: Enterprise detection and IDV are the most crowded categories in the brief, and every vendor claims 95-99% accuracy on its own test set. Buyers cannot compare products. Accuracy decays with each new generator, and injection attacks bypass isolated liveness checks. Model-risk officers must validate vendor models but have no independent evidence.
solution: Maintain a continuously refreshed attack corpus: newly released generators, voice clones degraded through phone codecs, virtual-camera and emulator injection, and re-compressed video. Test vendors black-box via API and publish false-accept rates at fixed false-reject rates, cross-generator drift, and time-to-fail after each new model release. Add model-risk documentation packs and court-ready error-rate statements. Vendors may pay only for private testing, never for ranking.
why_now: Detection vendors multiplied in 2025-26 and funding is still flowing (Modulate raised $25M). The injection-attack standard CEN/TS 18099 exists but has almost no commercial third-party lab. The EU AI Act transparency deadline on 2 Dec 2026 and rising fraud losses push buyers to demand proof.
revenue_model: $15-60K per year for full scorecards and monthly refreshes. Custom bake-offs for $25-100K. Expert-witness and litigation support as an upsell.
non_obvious_insight: In the 1990s, antivirus claims were unverifiable until independent labs became the arbiter. Deepfake detection is worse because accuracy decays with every new generator, so buyers need continuous evidence, which is a recurring-revenue product. The real asset is the fresh, hard-to-game attack corpus, and no vendor can build it credibly for itself.
first_30_days: Publish a free baseline report on 10 public detectors using about 300 fresh fakes from the newest open and commercial generators. Send it to 30 bank model-risk leads. Sign 3-5 design-partner subscriptions at about $10K each.

title: Factory-Slot Exchange for Transformers and Switchgear
one_liner: A verified marketplace and escrow for reassigning manufacturer production slots, the truly scarce asset, from stranded projects to shovel-ready buyers.
customer: Municipal utilities and rural electric co-ops that hyperscaler orders are crowding out, independent power producers, EPC procurement leads, and developers whose projects are stalled by moratoria or interconnection withdrawals and who hold deposit-backed slots they cannot use.
problem: Substation transformer lead times have stretched from about 140 weeks in 2023 to more than 160 weeks in 2026, and medium-voltage gear is at two to three years. Industry estimates say 30-50% of planned 2026 US data center capacity could slip on equipment alone. Slots are reserved years ahead with deposits, and when a project dies (a moratorium, a lost interconnection position) the slot is orphaned. Slot trading happens by handshake in whisper networks, with no verification and no title.
solution: A slot registry plus escrowed transfer. (1) Verify each slot with the manufacturer: spec, kVA and voltage class, delivery window, deposit status. (2) Get manufacturer consent, which is easier if you give them cleaner backlog data. (3) Match buyers using a small technical team of retired utility engineers who know which specs can be re-specified. (4) Hold funds in escrow and transfer title. Publish an index of slot pricing by spec, which is the first public price signal for the shortage.
why_now: Lead times are at record highs in 2026, and new state permit pauses (New York, Texas) are orphaning slots that speculative developers reserved. Small utilities lost their traditional access to equipment as hyperscalers bought capacity, which creates political goodwill for a neutral exchange.
revenue_model: A 2-4% fee on the purchase order value from the buyer and about 1% from the seller. Paid verification dossiers for sellers, and a subscription for the slot price index and alerts.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is the production slot with a spec, not the physical box. Because many slots can be re-specified within tolerance, a technical matchmaker unlocks supply that looks fungible only to insiders. The people hurt most, small utilities, are also the best-motivated and least-served buyers, so serving them is both profitable and defensible.
first_30_days: Recruit two retired utility procurement engineers as advisors. Cold-outreach 50 EPC procurement leads and 20 co-ops (start at NRECA-type meetings and LinkedIn). Collect five slot listings from stalled projects. Broker one transfer manually with a lawyer-drafted escrow agreement and no software. Charge the fee on that deal and use it as proof for the manufacturers.

title: Farm Income Dial: ACA Cliff Management
one_liner: A December planning service that uses the grain-contract and input-prepay levers farmers already control to keep household income under the 400% poverty cliff and avoid repaying a full year of health subsidies.
customer: Farm families who buy ACA marketplace coverage. KFF estimates about 27% of farmers do, nearly triple the adult average. The co-op grain desks and rural CPA firms that advise them pay for a white-label version.
problem: The enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025, so the hard cutoff at 400% of poverty is back (roughly $130k for a family of four). The 2025 tax law also removed repayment caps for tax year 2026. A farm family that projected income under the line and then lands $2,000 over must repay every dollar of advance credits, often $15k to $25k. Farm income is lumpy and depends on prices and yields nobody knows in January. Farm CPAs optimize the federal tax bracket, not the ACA cliff, and nobody connects the two.
solution: Farmers connect their grain settlements, deferred contracts, prepaid inputs and equipment purchases. The tool tracks estimated 2026 MAGI against the cliff and gives a concrete action list: how many bushels to defer into 2027, how much fertilizer to prepay, when to elect CCC loan treatment, when to buy equipment. It also models plan choice for 2027 open enrollment, including Farm Bureau non-ACA plans and their underwriting risks. Every recommendation is reviewed by the household's CPA, so this is planning software and not tax advice.
why_now: This is the first tax year with no repayment cap and no enhanced credits. Marketplace enrollment fell from 22.1M to 19.2M in a year. The planning window closes December 31, 2026, and every Iowa farm family on a marketplace plan is exposed right now.
revenue_model: $350 to $600 per farm household per season. Broker commissions from carriers when the tool places 2027 coverage. White-label licenses to rural CPA firms and co-op grain desks ($50 to $100 per client). Optional success fee of 10% of the protected credit.
non_obvious_insight: The ACA cliff is controlled with the same pen that signs deferred-payment contracts. The co-op grain desk is the real MAGI control panel for farm families. CPAs do not see it because they only meet clients in February, after the levers are gone.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 rural CPA firms and one co-op grain desk. Build a spreadsheet-grade calculator plus a one-page 'cliff letter' for clients. Run a 'Cliff Night' at the co-op with farm families in October and November. Convert 30 to 50 households at $350 before the December deadline and document dollars saved.

title: Second-Life Studio: Shelved Human Drugs for Dogs
one_liner: Mine the wreckage of failed human biotechs for safe, clinical-stage molecules that make viable dog and cat drugs, and broker them to animal-health companies.
customer: Animal-health business-development teams (Zoetis, Elanco, Dechra, Boehringer AH, Merck AH, Ceva, Virbac) and venture-backed vet-drug startups pay for screening and deal flow. Sellers (liquidating biotechs, bankruptcy trustees, pharma pruning portfolios) pay success fees.
problem: Roughly 300 'zombie' biotechs exist, and 2026 has brought 15,000+ biopharma job cuts across 50+ companies. Their clinical-stage compounds, with human safety and PK data in hand, are being abandoned because human markets need $300M+ peak sales. Meanwhile animal health has few new molecules for canine lymphoma and osteosarcoma, feline CKD, IBD or chronic pain, and about 80% of dogs with lymphoma never get IV chemo.
solution: A scouting and licensing studio. It uses AI to mine ClinicalTrials.gov, SEC filings, layoff and bankruptcy trackers for discontinued assets that were not stopped for safety. It scores each for target conservation in dogs and cats, allometric dosing, market size and eligibility for FDA CVM expanded conditional approval. It packages dossiers with a vet development plan and KOL letters, then brokers options, licenses or asset purchases, keeping a finder's fee plus equity or royalty in each spun-out newco.
why_now: The supply of stranded assets is at a peak (layoff tracker, 300 zombies, wobbling software-only AI-drug shops like Schrodinger). Precedents are proven: verdinexor, a human-oncology-origin XPO1 inhibitor, became the first oral canine lymphoma drug, and anti-NGF antibodies moved from human programs into dogs and cats. Pet owners increasingly want oncology and chronic-pain options, while roll-ups (GoodVets, Mars) create channels that can absorb new products.
revenue_model: $15-25k 'Vet Opportunity Screen' reports per target class. $25-100k option fees. Finder's fees of 2-5% of deal value, plus 5-10% equity or royalty in spun-out veterinary newcos.
non_obvious_insight: The human 'failure' threshold is a commercial threshold, not a biology threshold. A $50M-peak product is a rounding error to human pharma but a real business in companion animals, where the target biology is often the same. Zombie boards will sell for pennies, so a tiny studio can option assets that incumbents ignore.
first_30_days: Build a database of about 500 clinical-stage assets terminated since 2019 for non-safety reasons, and shortlist 30 with plausible vet indications. Email 15 liquidating boards and 10 animal-health BD leads. Sell the first two $15-25k target-class screens as paid retainers. Aim for the first option agreement within 4-6 months.

title: Insurer-Proof Watch Service for Inherited Houses
one_liner: A subscription that keeps a parent's empty house insured during probate by producing the dated inspection log insurers require, plus leak sensors and mail and utility handling.
customer: Adult children and executors managing a deceased or institutionalized parent's home from another city ($149-$249/month), reached through probate attorneys, realtors, senior move managers and estate-sale companies.
problem: Standard homeowner policies typically stop covering vandalism, theft and most water damage after 30-60 days of vacancy. Repairs from an undetected burst pipe run $10,000-$70,000 and claims have been denied at $60,000. Dedicated vacant-home policies cost roughly 25-60% more. Probate can bar sale for 9-18 months, so the house sits empty while heirs pay taxes, insurance and utilities and rarely visit.
solution: Weekly walk-throughs by vetted local checkers (off-duty inspectors, retirees) with timestamped photo and checklist logs in the format carriers accept. Add $30 cellular leak and freeze sensors, mail and utility management, seasonal tasks, and a monthly PDF the executor can hand to the insurer and the probate court. Broker partnerships handle the vacancy endorsement, and the service later hands off to cleanout and sale referrals.
why_now: The great wealth transfer is putting millions of parents' houses into estates. Cellular leak sensors are now $30, gig labor is easy to source, and homeowners carriers are tightening on vacancy as claims costs rise. Executors are increasingly remote adult children.
revenue_model: $149-$249/month subscription for 6-12 months (average lifetime about $1,500-$2,500), plus broker commission on vacancy endorsements and referral fees on cleanout and listing.
non_obvious_insight: Loss-adjuster guidance says the documentation that preserves coverage during vacancy is 'dated inspection photos with visit logs' plus utility and contractor records, so the inspection log itself is the product, and nobody sells it to heirs (https://vectorclaimsolutions.com/vacancy-clause-property-insurance/, which also cites a $60,000 vacancy-clause denial and 50-60% premiums for dedicated vacant policies). Carrying cost and vacancy-insurance friction for heirs is described at https://www.wedgewoodhomes.com/blog/vacant-house-insurance-inherited-home. Reddit was unreachable, so this is drawn from insurance and estate-practice sources describing the recurring 'we inherited Mom's house, now what?' thread pattern in r/AgingParents and r/homeowners.
first_30_days: Choose one metro. Recruit 5 checkers at about $35 per visit and buy 20 sensors. Pitch 15 probate attorneys and senior move managers with a one-page 'keep the house insured during probate' offer at $199/month. Sign 10 customers, verify with 2 carriers or agents that the log satisfies their vacancy conditions, and use that as the sales proof.

title: Resident Proof for Two-Tier Tourist Pricing
one_liner: A privacy-preserving QR proof of residence lets towns, museums and transit charge visitors more and locals less without building databases or discriminating by nationality.
customer: Municipalities and municipal attractions, ferries and parking in overrun towns of 5-100K people (Italy, Croatia, Spain, Japan), then private attractions and restaurants offering locals-first pricing.
problem: Insiders think dual pricing is a legal and PR minefield, useful only in niche places. It is spreading (reported moves include Rome's charge for non-resident visitors at the Trevi Fountain and resident-versus-visitor pricing at some Japanese castles). The real bottleneck is verification. Each site checks IDs by hand, builds a one-off app or discriminates crudely.
solution: Issue a wallet pass from the municipal residents' register, first over the town hall counter and later through national digital-ID wallets. It discloses only 'resident of X'. Gates and apps verify it offline, and the same pass unlocks locals-first booking windows and discounts. The town gets analytics on non-resident flows to tune fees.
why_now: Venice's flat fee reportedly did not reduce numbers, so cities are turning to differentiated pricing. EU member states must offer digital identity wallets by the end of 2026, which makes selective-disclosure credentials mainstream. Resident backlash is at its peak.
revenue_model: Municipal SaaS of EUR 10-30K per year, EUR 0.01-0.05 per verification, and an integration fee per attraction.
non_obvious_insight: Pricing policy is not the bottleneck; identity is. Whoever standardises the 'resident' claim owns the tollbooth for every future visitor-management rule, including resident-first windows, non-resident caps and local discounts.
first_30_days: Approach one town of 5-20K people that runs a municipal attraction, ferry or car park. Offer a free 90-day pilot where staff issue passes at the town hall and verify them with phone cameras. Use mayors' associations to find the pilot, and have a lawyer confirm the residency-based structure is proportionate.

title: Flood Cover Sold to the Lender
one_liner: Homeowners won't buy flood insurance, but the bank holding their mortgage should, because the uninsured flood loss lands on the lender's collateral.
customer: Community banks, credit unions and non-bank mortgage servicers with concentrated mortgage exposure outside FEMA high-risk zones, where flood cover isn't mandatory.
problem: Moody's puts uninsured US flood exposure at $375B-$1T. Private flood capacity is growing but 'customers aren't buying' (Insurance Business, 2026-07-22). Outside mandatory-purchase zones, borrowers skip cover, then walk or go delinquent after a flood and leave the lender with damaged collateral.
solution: Two steps. First, a parcel-level flood-exposure audit of the lender's book. Second, a lender-paid group or blanket flood policy (indemnity with a parametric fast-pay component) for the highest-risk non-mandatory loans, with disclosure and an opt-out. It is delivered as an MGA program on existing private flood capacity, and regulatory structure is validated state by state.
why_now: Private flood capacity is expanding (Neptune passed 300k policies and $400M premium). Reinsurance is softening, so capacity is cheap. Record cat bond issuance ($65.6B outstanding) shows abundant capital, and bank regulators are asking about climate concentration.
revenue_model: MGA commission and policy fees (roughly 10-20% of premium) plus a $15k-$40k paid portfolio audit per lender.
non_obvious_insight: The demand problem is really a distribution problem. Selling to 10,000 skeptical homeowners is expensive, while selling to one lender covers thousands of borrowers. The party with the incentive to buy is the one who bears the unmandated loss.
first_30_days: Run free flood-exposure audits for 20 credit unions in river and Gulf states using public mortgage data and open flood models. Line up a licensed surplus-lines partner. Sell one paid pilot covering about 500 highest-risk loans.

title: First-72-Hours Concierge for Paid Communities
one_liner: An outcome-priced service that staffs experienced ex-power-mods to personally handle every new member's first three days in creator-run paid communities, cutting the week-one churn that drains recurring revenue.
customer: Owners of paid communities with 500-20,000 paying members on Skool, Circle, Discord, Mighty Networks or Patreon: course creators and trading, fitness and business coaches doing $50k-$1M+ per month.
problem: Skool operator guides say about 60% of churners decide in week one, and average monthly churn sits around 12-18%. Owners cover the front door with random volunteers or VAs posting templated welcomes. New members' first posts go unanswered for a day. Scam DMs from fake admins ('send USDT to verify') hit newcomers hardest. The first unexplained removal or cold reply turns a paying member into a refund request.
solution: Small pods of trained ex-moderators run the first 72 hours: a personal welcome, a reply to every first post within 2 hours across time zones, routing to the right thread, removal of impersonators and scam DMs, and gentle handling of first-time rule breaks so the person stays. AI drafts and triages, but a human always sends. Each community gets a rules-as-code playbook and a weekly cohort-retention report with a holdout group so the effect is measurable. Work stays on Discord, Skool and Circle, so it doesn't collide with Reddit's Rule 5.
why_now: Reddit began enforcing its five-community moderator cap on 31 March 2026. That has pushed many experienced volunteer mods into Advisor/Alumni roles and left them open to paid work on platforms the cap doesn't cover. Creator-run paid communities have grown into real revenue businesses, while AI slop and scam DMs make the new-member experience worse.
revenue_model: A base fee of $1.5k-$4k per month per community plus an outcome kicker of 10-20% of retained MRR uplift versus a holdout. Mods are paid $15-$25 per hour, giving roughly 40-50% gross margin.
non_obvious_insight: In big subreddits a newcomer whose first comment is removed without explanation almost never returns. Retention is decided in the first three days by one human interaction, not by content quality. That makes moderation a retention function, not a cost center, so it should be priced by churn saved, not hours worked. It is also hard to outsource to a generic trust-and-safety BPO, because tone and judgment are the product.
first_30_days: Recruit 10-15 ex-power-mods from mod Discords and r/ModSupport who lost seats under the cap. Write a one-page playbook. Approach 30 owners of Skool communities with 1k+ paying members, using the public discovery listings. Offer a $750, 14-day pilot in which half of new joiners get the concierge and half don't. Report the day-14 retention delta and convert the best results into monthly contracts.

title: Pet Evacuation Capacity Options
one_liner: An annual small-fee option that reserves boarding capacity near you and pays for it automatically when an official evacuation order hits your address.
customer: Pet-owning households in wildfire, hurricane and flood zones, especially those on FAIR plans or recently nonrenewed. Homeowner insurers, brokers and HOAs are second buyers as a retention perk. Boarding kennels, vet clinics and pet-friendly hotels sell the reserved capacity.
problem: Pets are a leading reason people delay or refuse evacuation. In an evacuation the scarce resource is capacity, not money: pet-friendly shelters fill within hours and boarding facilities book out. Homeowners facing record nonrenewals have no cheap product to show insurers are still doing something for them, and kennels' unused capacity is perishable inventory.
solution: Sell an annual $49-79 option: reserved boarding slots (up to 14 days at a pre-agreed rate) at a vetted network within a 2-hour drive. It is triggered automatically when an official evacuation warning polygon covers the owner's address. Vaccination records are pre-verified so facilities accept the pet immediately. Facilities earn a retainer for reserving capacity plus a surge rate when exercised, paid instantly. Launch as a prepaid service reservation and convert to a parametric insurance structure through an MGA later.
why_now: Homeowner nonrenewals set records, California passed three claims and nonrenewal bills on Sept 3, and FAIR plans are growing. Reinsurance is softening with record cat-bond issuance, so parametric capacity is cheap. Instant payment rails exist, and late September is the run-up to peak fire and hurricane exposure.
revenue_model: Annual option premium, B2B2C fees of $10-20 per policy from insurers, brokers or HOAs, and a margin on surge-rate exercises.
non_obvious_insight: Sell a call option on capacity, not an insurance payout. In a crisis the value is in a guaranteed place to put the animal, and kennels would rather sell perishable capacity in advance than hope for demand. Parametric triggers make the whole thing automatic, which insurers love.
first_30_days: Pick one wildfire county. Sign 8 boarding facilities on a small retainer and pre-sell 300 households through fire-safe councils and HOAs. Build the trigger from public evacuation-zone feeds and run reservations manually the first season.

title: Model-Swap Regression Service for Contractors
one_liner: Automated testing and porting that lets defense contractors re-platform their AI workflows to a different model vendor in weeks without losing quality.
customer: Defense integrators, primes' AI teams and mid-size government contractors whose workflows were tuned around one model family and must now change vendors.
problem: The D.C. Circuit upheld the DoD supply-chain-risk designation of one model vendor on Sept 26, and DoD is moving classified workloads off it by October. Contractors are cutting that vendor's use. Their prompts, agents and evaluation sets were tuned for one model, and nobody can prove a replacement performs equally on their real tasks.
solution: Capture the contractor's existing workflow traces, build a task-specific eval set, run it across Gemini, ChatGPT, Grok and open-weight models, and auto-rewrite prompts and tool schemas to reach parity. Deliver a signed parity report usable as evidence for the government customer.
why_now: The designation is a fresh legal fact with an October deadline. Vendor politics now shape the supply chain, and lawful-use terms differ by vendor. Model swapping is now a compliance event, not an engineering preference.
revenue_model: $40-200K per migration project, then $3-10K per month for continuous cross-vendor regression monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: The designation is not a one-time event. Every future vendor dispute will force the same migration, so the durable product is a standing eval-and-port harness for a politically volatile model market.
first_30_days: Post a fixed-price migration audit at $15K. Contact 15 small integrators and GenAI.mil agent builders through defense AI communities. Reuse one eval harness across clients while keeping each client's data separate.

title: Robot Finger That Makes Legacy Instruments Agent-Operable
one_liner: A camera-plus-servo retrofit box that presses buttons, turns knobs and reads displays on validated lab and test equipment from the outside, giving decade-old instruments an API without touching their software.
customer: QC and analytical labs in pharma and CDMOs, food and environmental testing labs, university core facilities, and small biotechs running out-of-support equipment such as plate readers, autoclaves, centrifuges, HPLC pumps, stability chambers and test benches.
problem: Lab automation assumes new, API-enabled instruments, but the installed base is 10-20-year-old boxes with front panels only. In GxP and ISO 17025 labs, changing instrument firmware or software can trigger revalidation, which blocks IT-style integration. Scientists and agents still want unattended overnight runs, scheduling and structured logs.
solution: A clamp-on or adhesive module with 2-6 servos for buttons, knobs and a touchscreen stylus, a wide-angle camera, and a vision-language model that reads 7-segment displays, LCDs and status LEDs. A confirm-after-every-action loop and hard interlocks make it safe. It exposes an MCP and REST endpoint ('start program 4', 'read temperature', 'log state') and keeps video plus state log as the audit trail. It sits outside the validated boundary as 'operator-equivalent', so only the actuator needs qualification.
why_now: Vision-language models now read messy panels cheaply and reliably, and servo and edge-compute costs are trivial. Autonomous-lab offerings such as Ginkgo Cloud Lab prove scientists want agent-run experiments, but they require shipping samples to a vendor's lab. Most labs still own and must keep using their own equipment.
revenue_model: $400-900 hardware per instrument, $40-100 per month per device for scheduling, audit trail and the agent endpoint, and $2-5k per site for IQ/OQ qualification templates.
non_obvious_insight: Revalidation cost, not technology, blocks lab automation. An actuator that does exactly what a technician's finger does sidesteps change control, so selling 'validation-friendly' beats selling 'smart'. The video-verified state log is also a better audit trail than most instruments produce natively.
first_30_days: Build 3 prototypes from off-the-shelf servos, cameras and a Raspberry Pi-class board. Interview 20 QC lab managers and core-facility directors. Offer free two-week pilots on one autoclave or plate reader that runs a nightly routine, then convert to a $3k paid pilot including an IQ/OQ document.

title: Smell Graders for Recycled Plastic
one_liner: A network of trained human noses that gives every batch of post-consumer recycled plastic an odor grade from 1 to 5, creating the price tier and spec that brands need to hit recycled-content mandates.
customer: Plastic recyclers selling PCR resin (HDPE, PP), converters that mold bottles and tubs, and brand owners in personal care, household and food buying PCR under EU and US recycled-content rules. The recyclers' quality managers buy first, then brand procurement teams.
problem: Odor is one of the biggest barriers to using recycled plastic. Recyclers can't tell buyers reliably what a batch smells like. Brands reject loads or cap PCR percentages out of caution. Lab methods such as GC-olfactometry are slow and costly, and there's no shared odor grade the way coffee has the Q-score.
solution: A standard protocol (heated headspace jars, blind triplicates, a reference odor kit, descriptor vocabulary such as rancid, detergent, smoky) run by a panel of trained sniffers recruited from perfumers, coffee Q-graders, sommeliers and food-sensory panelists. Recyclers mail samples and get a 48-hour graded report. Human scores then train an e-nose and GC model that lowers cost per test. Over time it becomes a certification: license and train graders, and publish the grade spec brands cite in purchase contracts.
why_now: The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation applies from 12 August 2026, with 2030 recycled-content minimums (30% for contact-sensitive PET, 10% for other contact-sensitive plastics). Brands have to buy far more PCR within a few years. Sensor vendors need human-panel labels to train on, and none has a standard odor tier to price against.
revenue_model: $120 to $250 per batch grade. Weekly-lot subscriptions for recyclers. Vendor-qualification programs for brands at $30k or more per year. Grader certification and training fees. Licensing of the labeled dataset to e-nose makers.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation mandates recycled content, but a human nose decides whether the resin is usable, and buyers will not trust a grade until someone standardizes it. Whoever owns the grading standard sets the price tiers for the whole PCR market, a bit like coffee's Q-grading. Human panels remain the legal and commercial ground truth even after e-noses arrive.
first_30_days: Recruit 12 sniffers from local specialty roasters and perfume or flavor schools. Buy vials, a hot plate and a reference odor kit for under $1,000. Offer three regional recyclers free grading of 20 batches each, and check the grades against their buyers' rejection history. Then price it. Publish a free 'PCR smell atlas' to attract recycler and brand inbound.

title: Paid Farm Residencies That Recruit Successors
one_liner: Multi-week hospitality-designed farm stays that let heir-less owners audition would-be farmers, monetising the stay and taking a success fee if a lease-to-own follows.
customer: Owners aged 65+ of orchards, vineyards, dairies and livestock farms with no heir, plus career-changing or remote-working would-be farmers with capital who pay for the residency. Farm Credit lenders and estate lawyers are referral partners.
problem: About one-third of US farmers have no obvious heir, and only about 1 in 4 has a formal succession plan. Over 60% of farmland may change hands in 10-15 years, much of it through estates that listing sites never see. Existing matching programs are listing databases, so skill and personal fit stay unresolved until people actually work together, and farm incomes are squeezed by input costs.
solution: Run 2-4 week residencies at $3K-$6K per guest with lodging, meals, remote-work setup (Starlink and a desk), and structured farm-management workshops on finances, equipment and land tenure. A shortlisted guest can take a paid trial season as a W-2 employee. Provide lender introductions (beginning-farmer loans) and lease-to-own and Buy-Protect-Sell templates, and take a success fee at transition. Winter orchard and vineyard pruning gives a bookable season within six months.
why_now: Remote work and nomad visas created the first cohort able to relocate to a farm without quitting a job. Bankruptcies up 19% and a fourth straight year of row-crop losses are pushing owners to plan exits, and the 'invisible transfer' wave means estates, not listings, decide who gets land. AI-assistant booking now lets tiny hosts sell stays directly.
revenue_model: Guest fees of $3K-$6K. A $750 farmer onboarding fee. A success fee of $15K-$25K or 1-2% of land or lease value at transition.
non_obvious_insight: Successors are not found in databases but in the third week of living together, so hospitality is the screening technology. The stay revenue pays the retiring farmer to audition candidates instead of paying a broker, and the trust built also unlocks the seller-financing that beginning farmers usually lack.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 specialty farms with owners aged 65+ in the Hudson Valley, Vermont, the Willamette Valley and Michigan. Open applications through career-change and nomad newsletters, and pre-sell 20 winter-pruning residencies for Dec-Mar.

title: Blank-and-Recipe Kits for Desktop UV Printer Owners
one_liner: A monthly kit of pre-cut blanks, matched jigs and pre-calibrated height maps for the roughly 23,000 desktop UV printers that crowdfunding put into homes, so owners can fill machines and sell without fixturing trial-and-error.
customer: Owners of eufyMake E1, Longer ePrint and HeyGears-class desktop UV printers: Etsy and craft-fair sellers, keycap and phone-case micro-brands, makerspaces. Payer is the printer owner running a side business.
problem: Owners paid $1,500-$2,700 for a machine but still need to source consistent blanks, build registration jigs, tune 2.5D height maps, and finish for durability. Files are sold ad hoc on Etsy, but the hard part is physical fixturing and repeatability, so machines sit idle.
solution: A subscription that ships 30-50 laser-cut or CNC blanks (acrylic coasters, aluminium tags, keycaps, phone-case shells), a laser-cut alignment jig sized to the printer's bed, and a bundled PNG plus height map plus 'recipe card' (curing, primer and clear-coat steps) tested on the E1 and Longer. Add wholesale blank packs for sellers who want to scale, plus a 'sell this next' trend drop based on Etsy search data.
why_now: eufyMake E1 became Kickstarter's most funded project ever ($46.76M, 17,822 backers), Longer added $4.2M (1,584 backers) and HeyGears G1 $17.4M (3,911 backers). Units delivered from late 2025 through 2026 mean roughly 23,000 new owners are hitting the practical limits of the hobby now, and Etsy already has listings for E1 jigs and height-map bundles.
revenue_model: $59/mo blank-and-recipe kit, $0.40-$1.20 per blank wholesale packs (55-65% gross margin), and $19 add-on jig files. Later, sell a validated-blank certification to printer makers.
non_obvious_insight: Files are already a commodity on Etsy (e.g. 'Full Honor Set' bundles with PNG, Height Map, Print Guide, and popular E1 jigs, https://www.etsy.com/market/uv_printer_file), and the printer makers fight over ink instead. Owners' real pain is physical: one review notes prints need protective finishing, flat prints take minutes but textured pieces close to an hour, and heavy users hit ink-expiry chips (about GBP 240 of dead ink after seven months, https://www.makerhacks.com/eufymake-e1-review/), which a GitHub project was created to work around (https://github.com/joggie/eufy-timewarp). The same review says the business is 'high margin, low volume' (a keychain costing 85p sells for GBP 10-15; a GBP 5-8 tumbler up to GBP 25). Sellers who scale need repeatable blanks and jigs more than another file, and a consumable-with-recipe product is sold to them, not to the vendor. Demand sizing: https://www.entrepreneur.com/business-news/3d-printer-breaks-kickstarter-record-raises-44m/493857 and https://www.gizmocrowd.com/top-crowdfunding-campaigns.
first_30_days: Buy one E1-class printer (or borrow from an owner) and produce 3 kit designs: acrylic keychain, aluminium tag, keycap. Sell 50 founding kits at $49 in the eufyMake users Facebook group and r/UVprinting. Share before/after photos and per-piece margin math. Use a local laser-cut shop for blanks and collect feedback to lock registration tolerances.

title: Evacuation Lift Registry Ending Double-Booked Buses
one_liner: A neutral county-level registry that guarantees each ambulance, wheelchair van and bus seat is promised to only one nursing home per storm, paid for by facilities and by carriers who finally get standby retainers.
customer: Paying: multi-site nursing home and assisted-living operators (SaaS per facility) and ambulance/NEMT/charter-bus operators (platform fee on standby retainers). Sponsoring: county emergency managers and healthcare coalitions using preparedness grants.
problem: The CMS emergency preparedness rule makes every facility hold transportation agreements, but no one checks whether the same 40 wheelchair vans and ambulances are 'contracted' by 300 facilities. GAO and post-Katrina research found carriers holding contracts with many facilities in one community, which works for a single-building evacuation and collapses when a whole county goes at once. Facilities learn at H-48 that their contract is one of a dozen identical promises. Carriers do not honor a promise they were never paid to hold.
solution: Borrow the military's lift-allocation discipline, where an asset can appear on the movement plan only once. Facilities reserve capacity by resident mix (ambulatory, wheelchair, stretcher, oxygen or vent-dependent), not by 'beds'. The registry totals promised demand against real vehicle capacity by county and flags oversubscription weeks before the season, then matches the gap to out-of-region carriers on paid standby. At activation it issues a departure-window movement table so convoys do not collide, plus manifest and accountability packets for each facility. Before activation it stores only aggregate counts by acuity, not PHI, which keeps HIPAA scope small.
why_now: The President's FEMA Review Council final report (May 7, 2026) recommends disaster response be 'locally executed, state managed, federally supported'. Counties and healthcare coalitions are inheriting logistics they never staffed, with less federal backfill. It is peak hurricane season, and post-acute care closures and consolidation are concentrating residents into fewer, larger buildings.
revenue_model: $150-400 per facility per month. Carriers pay 8-12% on standby retainers the platform brokers, which they never received before. Optional county or coalition license of $25-100k a year, funded by ASPR HPP or EMPG grants. Later, add-ons for dialysis centers, group homes and inpatient rehab.
non_obvious_insight: Vehicles are not the shortage. Unique promises are. Every evacuation failure post-mortem says 'not enough buses', but the fleet often exists and is simply committed many times over. Military movement planners never let one lift asset appear twice on a time-phased deployment plan, while civilian planners have nobody whose job is to check. Loading time is also the hidden constraint: a stretcher resident takes about 20 minutes to load, so acuity mix, not headcount, determines how many vehicles you need.
first_30_days: Pick one storm-prone county cluster (Tampa Bay, coastal Carolinas or Louisiana parishes). Ask 10 facilities to share their transport MOUs, which they must keep on file for CMS surveys anyway. Build the overlap heat map by hand in a spreadsheet, for example 'nine of your ten facilities are promised the same carrier'. Take it to the county emergency manager and the healthcare coalition coordinator. Convert 3-5 facilities to a paid pilot at about $200 a month and sign 2 carriers to retainer contracts. Build the product as Airtable plus a simple web form before writing real software.

title: Estate Planning for People's AI Agents
one_liner: Powers of attorney, dead-man switches and revocation tooling for the agents that hold standing authority over your money, email and subscriptions.
customer: Estate-planning attorneys and RIAs or family offices serving tech founders and executives who already run personal agents, followed by consumers through those channels.
problem: Personal agents now hold standing authority: card mandates, wallets, email access, autopay and negotiations. Step two: authority is tied to a living principal. Step three: death, incapacity, divorce or bankruptcy leaves agents acting on stale instructions or locks heirs out. Fiduciary access laws (for example RUFADAA) give no automatic access to digital accounts, and nobody has drafted for delegated software.
solution: An Agent Schedule for estate plans. It combines an inventory of agents, OAuth grants, wallets and mandates (via connectors), attorney-drafted clauses giving a digital fiduciary authority to pause, transfer or delete agents and limiting post-death actions, an incapacity or dead-man trigger that rotates credentials and downgrades permissions to read-only while notifying the fiduciary, and export of agent memory and logs for the executor.
why_now: Personal agents went mainstream in 2026 (OpenClaw reached about 247k GitHub stars), and agentic wallets and machine-payment rails launched in February and March 2026. The estate bar is only starting to publish AI afterlife primers, and they focus on AI personas, not delegated agents.
revenue_model: $500-$1,500 per client schedule sold through attorneys (roughly $300 wholesale), $10-$30/month monitoring, and $5k/year RIA channel licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Every technology that received delegated authority (checks, credit cards, cloud accounts) eventually got a legal instrument for the case where the principal stops existing. Agents have none yet, and the trigger events are guaranteed, so demand arrives on a calendar.
first_30_days: Draft the template with 2 estate attorneys. Pilot with 10 founders through an existing network. Build a simple inventory and revocation checklist using OAuth grant discovery for Google, Microsoft 365, GitHub and 5 agent platforms, and charge $750 per pilot.

title: Permit-as-Firmware Groundwater Pump Governor
one_liner: A smart pump controller that hard-enforces a farmer's groundwater allocation and lets an agent trade unused acre-feet with neighbors before the pump ever exceeds its limit.
customer: Irrigated growers (almonds, pistachios, alfalfa, wine grapes) in California's regulated groundwater basins, especially San Joaquin Valley subbasins with adopted allocations and overpumping penalties. Groundwater sustainability agencies (GSAs) are the channel and co-payer.
problem: Allocations are enforced after the fact from meter reads. Kings County's agency, for example, set a $500-per-acre-foot charge for pumping above base allocation, with penalties slated after the 2026 water year. Probationary subbasins (Tule, Tulare Lake) add $300-per-well registration and a $20-per-acre-foot state fee. Farmers overshoot by accident, water trades run through brokers and phone calls, and GSAs cannot verify compliance without costly audits.
solution: A retrofit device on the well's starter or VFD, tied to a certified flow-meter reader, keeping a live allocation ledger. It soft-throttles as the budget nears zero, and can hard-stop with a paid override that 'borrows' at the penalty price. The grower's dashboard or agent can pre-bid to buy or sell units on a subbasin exchange. The GSA receives a read-only, tamper-evident compliance feed and can give fee discounts for participating wells.
why_now: Allocation-based enforcement begins in earnest with the 2027 water year, and the state has already put two San Joaquin Valley subbasins on probation. Water prices and fallowing pressure make trading valuable. Cellular and LoRa IoT and smart motor starters are now cheap.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k per well install, $50-150 per month per well, a 1-2% fee on water trades, and GSA grants or fee credits that subsidise compliance metering.
non_obvious_insight: The law is already a constraint. The product turns a legal budget into a physical budget, like a hard credit limit on a card. Growers want the stop because it converts unpredictable $500-per-acre-foot penalties into a controllable budget, and GSAs want it because self-reporting becomes verified data. Sell it as insurance against fines, not as smart irrigation.
first_30_days: Pick one subbasin with adopted allocations and penalties. Recruit 3 pump-service companies as install partners, since they own the relationship with the well. Pilot free on 5 wells in exchange for testimonials and data. Ask the GSA general manager for a compliance-metering pilot grant.

title: Independent Accuracy Certification for Wearable Health Claims
one_liner: A third-party lab that certifies wearable metrics (HRV, sleep staging, BP trends) now that the FDA has stepped back, funded by makers and trusted by buyers.
customer: Wearable and health-app makers selling into employers, payers, clinics, coaches and gyms (they pay for certification). Secondary: self-insured employers, payers and coaching platforms that subscribe to procurement-grade reports.
problem: Insiders cheered the FDA's January 2026 General Wellness guidance as freedom. But no clearance means no trusted filter: buyers cannot tell which of dozens of rings, watches and patches are accurate, one analysis argued wearables 'beat the FDA and lost the insurance money', and makers have no credible third-party proof to show payers. Claims exposure to the FTC, state AGs and class actions rises at the same time.
solution: Run a standing panel of about 200 volunteers with lab-grade references (ECG chest strap, a partner polysomnography lab, clinical and ambulatory BP, VO2/lactate testing). Test devices and features under a published protocol, issue tiered 'Verified for [metric]' marks with stated error bands (re-tested at major firmware changes), publish a public leaderboard, and sell buyers a procurement report they can cite in RFPs.
why_now: FDA's Jan 2026 wellness guidance lets physiologic-metric features (HRV, SpO2, BP trends) skip review; Whoop's BP feature drew a July 2025 warning letter and a June 2026 closeout; the HIPRA consumer-health-data bill cleared Senate HELP 22-0 on July 30, 2026, so scrutiny of wearable data is rising while the FDA filter is gone.
revenue_model: Certification fees of $15-60k per device or feature per year with re-test fees; $5-25k/yr buyer subscriptions for procurement reports; per-test fees for startups needing payer credibility.
non_obvious_insight: Deregulation does not remove the need for a trust filter, it privatizes it. The certifier is paid by makers but its only currency is buyer trust, so it must publish unflattering results (Consumer Reports crossed with a safety-lab model). Whoever writes the reference protocol first gets cited in payer and employer RFPs, which is a durable moat.
first_30_days: Partner with a university exercise-physiology or sleep lab, recruit 40 volunteers, test 6 popular rings/watches on resting HR, HRV and sleep staging against ECG/PSG, publish the methodology and preliminary results, then sell 2-3 employer-facing wearable startups a paid $15k pre-publication verification.

title: Hidden Satellite Tags Against Fictitious Pickups
one_liner: A cargo custody kit that pairs a verified-carrier check at pickup with several disposable Bluetooth-to-satellite tags hidden in each load, giving brokers and insurers evidence of where freight went when it was stolen.
customer: Mid-size freight brokers (20-200 staff) and 3PLs moving theft-prone loads (electronics, pharma, beverages, copper) on US and cross-border lanes, and inland-marine cargo insurers or MGAs that have raised deductibles on theft. Start with brokers hit by fictitious pickups.
problem: Thieves impersonate legitimate carriers and dispatchers (increasingly with cloned voices), pick up loads and vanish. The one expensive GPS tracker per trailer is found and jammed, cell-based devices fail in remote drop points, and the broker learns hours later. Paperwork chains are spoofable, and insurers cannot prove the exact custody break.
solution: (1) An identity gate at pickup that partners with existing carrier-verification vendors (MC/DOT match, live driver ID, verified call-back). (2) Three to five disposable $5-12 Bluetooth-to-satellite tags bound to the bill of lading at pickup and hidden in cartons. (3) An evidence timeline of last-seen sightings from orbit, including where there is no cell coverage, compared against the declared route. (4) Police-ready location packets and an insurer-accepted custody report that earns premium credits.
why_now: Bluetooth-to-satellite just crossed into serious capital: Hubble Network raised a $200M Series C at a $1.6B valuation on 28 Sept 2026, with 6 satellites up and a next generation in 2027 aiming at much lower-power detection. Cheaper launch is collapsing per-tag and per-message costs. Voice-clone impersonation and business email compromise ($3.05B in US losses) make carrier identity fraud easier.
revenue_model: $12-25 per protected load with volume tiers, an insurer revenue share on premium credits, and annual platform fees for brokers with more than 5,000 loads.
non_obvious_insight: Trackers fail because thieves can find and defeat the single expensive device. When a tag costs $6 and needs no phone network, a broker can hide many of them, and abundance beats stealth. Current sat-BLE revisit times are hours, so the product is priced as last-seen evidence and recovery, not live tracking. The true buyer is often the insurer, who values proof of the custody-break moment.
first_30_days: Buy 500 tags through the vendor developer program. Recruit 3 brokers via freight-intermediary association networks. Tag every load on their two highest-theft lanes at cost for 30 days and log coverage and gaps. Bring the results to two cargo MGAs and negotiate a premium-credit pilot.

title: Local-Law Radar for Data Center and Battery Developers
one_liner: A system that continuously reads city and county codes, planning agendas and minutes nationwide and warns developers which jurisdictions are drafting moratoria or new setback, noise and fire-safety rules before they pass.
customer: Land-acquisition and permitting teams at data-center, battery-storage, solar, EV-charging and peaker developers, siting consultants, and law-firm land-use groups.
problem: Local ordinances decide whether $100M-$1B projects get built, but roughly 19,000 municipalities publish codes and agendas as PDFs on inconsistent sites. Opposition-driven moratoria appear with weeks of notice, developers learn about them after buying land options, and existing zoning datasets capture setbacks and floor-area ratios, not conditional-use or moratorium rules for new infrastructure types.
solution: A scraper and LLM pipeline over municipal-code hosts and agenda platforms (Legistar, CivicClerk, PrimeGov and similar) that classifies items by project type, alerts on early signals ('first reading', 'study session', 'interim urgency ordinance'), answers 'is X permitted at parcel Y and under what conditions?', and scores county risk. Two land-use paralegals curate the output.
why_now: Data-center and battery-storage siting fights surged through 2025-26, including after the Jan 2025 Moss Landing battery fire (background, verify), and LLMs can now read messy municipal PDFs cheaply enough to cover thousands of jurisdictions.
revenue_model: $2-10k/month per developer team, $60-250k/year enterprise plans, and $500-2,000 per-parcel reports.
non_obvious_insight: Moratoria are telegraphed weeks ahead in public agendas that nobody reads at scale, so the value is the leading indicator, not the code text. A stranded land option costs far more than the subscription.
first_30_days: Cover the three states with the most data-center activity and track about 500 jurisdictions' agendas. Publish a weekly free moratorium tracker, sell five developers or site-selection consultants at $2.5k/month, and back-test which past moratoria would have been flagged 30 days early.

title: Work-Share Desk: Kurzarbeit for American Employers
one_liner: Administer state short-time compensation for mid-size employers so they can cut hours 20-40% instead of laying off skilled staff, with workers drawing pro-rated unemployment benefits.
customer: Employers with 50-800 employees (manufacturers, distributors, engineering firms, PEO-served businesses) in states with work-share programs, buying through the CFO, HR head or PEO.
problem: Roughly 33 states have short-time compensation programs, yet take-up is tiny because employers do not know they exist and the paperwork (plan applications, weekly certifications, state-specific rules, payroll integration) is painful. Layoffs then destroy trained staff who cost one to two times salary to replace when demand returns.
solution: A layoff-versus-work-share calculator for CFOs, plus a done-for-you service. It checks eligibility, prepares the state plan, connects payroll (Gusto, ADP, Rippling) to generate weekly certification data, provides employee communication scripts and tracks the effect on the employer's unemployment account. Expand state by state and through PEOs and manufacturers' associations.
why_now: The oil shock (crude above $100, diesel near $6) and the September 2026 Fed hike, the first since 2023, are cooling consumers. Unemployment is still low at about 4.1%, so executives want to keep hard-to-replace workers and are wary of repeating the 2022-2023 layoff-then-rehire cycle.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 setup fee plus $10-15 per participating employee per week, or 15% of verified savings versus layoff and rehire. PEO channel revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The program exists but nobody built the admin layer because the payoff only arrives in downturns. This is a business that sells the same product every recession and can build its state-rule database and PEO channel during the quiet years. Retention value is high precisely because the labor market is still tight.
first_30_days: Pick two manufacturing-heavy states with simple program rules (for example Ohio, Michigan or Pennsylvania). Publish a free layoff-versus-work-share calculator. Pitch 30 manufacturers via associations and PEOs and sign 5-10 at a $1,500 flat setup fee, doing the paperwork by hand at first.

title: Dispute Escrow for Agent Payments on Pix/UPI
one_liner: A neutral hold-and-evidence layer that gives agent-initiated Pix and UPI payments the dispute protection cards have and push rails never did.
customer: Brazilian WhatsApp-commerce, bill-pay and shopping-agent startups and their sponsoring payment institutions, plus Indian UPI apps building agentic checkout. Marketplaces and merchants who want to accept agent buyers are the second payer.
problem: Pix, UPI and M-Pesa are push rails: instantly final, with no chargeback culture. When an agent buys the wrong SKU, gets prompt-injected, or loops, the money is simply gone. Visa and Mastercard still have no binding agent-chargeback rule, and the ledger shows only amount, time and merchant, with no record of why the agent paid. Merchants cannot tell a legitimate agent buyer from an abusive one, and PSPs cannot price the risk.
solution: An API that wraps agent-initiated push payments in a short programmable hold (2-24h) through a licensed partner PSP's escrow or split-payment accounts, or through UPI block-and-debit mandates. Each payment carries a signed 'decision receipt': the user's mandate, a hash of the agent's tool-call trace, price-check evidence and model version. A small human adjudication desk releases or refunds by published rules. PSPs, merchants and insurers all accept the receipt as evidence. The SDK is free; money movement and adjudication are the paid layer.
why_now: Agent rails (AP2 mandates, Mastercard Verifiable Intent, MPP, x402, ACP/UCP) all solve authorization but none define fault or evidence for push rails. India ends zero-MDR UPI for large P2M payments on Oct 15, and a rail that starts charging merchants acquires card-like dispute expectations. Insurers are adding AI exclusions, so they need telemetry to price anything. The Ninth Circuit's 'the agent is the user' ruling pushes liability toward users and their intermediaries.
revenue_model: 0.2-0.4% of held volume, $0.02-0.05 per receipt at scale, and dispute-handling fees paid by whichever side loses. Later, an evidence-pack license to PSPs and insurers underwriting agent risk.
non_obvious_insight: In emerging markets most digital volume rides rails with no chargeback system, so agent error is an unhedged first-class risk there. Whoever holds the neutral, tamper-evident record of why an agent paid becomes the arbiter, and eventually the underwriter, for every party. The cards networks are structurally slow to solve this for rails they do not run.
first_30_days: Publish an open-source decision-receipt SDK for agents that pay via Pix or UPI. Recruit 10 small agent builders (WhatsApp bill-pay and shopping bots) on developer communities. Sign one licensed PSP for escrow sandbox accounts. Hand-adjudicate the first 100 disputes yourselves to learn the fault taxonomy, then price the hold as a paid tier.

title: Bring-Into-Use Satellites for Spectrum Filing Holders
one_liner: Fixed-price rideshare satellites that let holders of valuable spectrum and orbit filings meet ITU hardware milestones instead of losing them.
customer: Telecom ministries and regulators of small and mid-size states (Gulf, Africa, Pacific, Central Asia, Latin America), plus startups that hold NGSO filings but cannot afford a full constellation.
problem: Spectrum and orbit rights are now priced like beachfront (EchoStar's reported $23B sale to AT&T and $17B sale to SpaceX), yet ITU rules still require real hardware in orbit by set deadlines. A holder of paper filings is one missed milestone from losing the asset, and a real constellation costs hundreds of millions.
solution: A standard 6U-12U bus with a software-defined payload configurable to the filed bands, sold as a 'milestone in a box'. The package covers rideshare launch, operations, evidence for the administration and coordination paperwork. Regulatory counsel decides what counts as bringing into use for each filing. Entry product is a filing-health audit built from public ITU data.
why_now: The 2025-26 EchoStar deals reset what spectrum is worth. Rideshare is plentiful (321 orbital launches in 2025 per the briefing). Commercial 6U buses and SDR payloads are off the shelf, and nine-figure rounds at European bus makers show integration capacity is growing. Sovereign space programs are multiplying.
revenue_model: Audit $20-50k. Fixed-price milestone satellite $1.5-4M. Annual retainer of $100-300k for filing maintenance and coordination. Optional success fee when a preserved filing is sold or leased.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders treat filings as paper assets and hardware as optional. The ITU makes hardware the price of keeping the paper, so the scarce thing is cheap, compliant placeholder hardware plus the regulatory playbook. Nobody sells that as a product.
first_30_days: Hire one ex-administration or ITU filing specialist on contract. Scrape public ITU filing data and rank about 100 filings by deadline urgency. Send personalized audits to 50 administrations and startups, and charge for the first five. Collect LOI-backed pre-orders before committing to hardware.
